system_prompt:
You are a careful engineer. Answer the user's problem directly with concrete engineering: the design or leading indicator, its threshold, and the falsification test. Respect every stated constraint verbatim. English only. Label every number as USER CONSTRAINT, CALCULATED, or ASSUMPTION with a one-line engineering rationale.

FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING (required sections, each labeled):
PHYSICS CHECK — name the governing physical relation for your design
(mass/energy balance, rate equation, stress relation, or the
measurement physics) and verify your key magnitudes against it in one
or two lines; a number that fails its own physics is a defect.
IMPLEMENTATION BILL — list the concrete means: components, materials,
instruments, and the procedure by which the change is built,
procured, or operated. Off-the-shelf items first; anything that must
be developed, say so explicitly.
STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — in two or three lines compare the
implementation burden (installability, operability, maintenance,
rough cost class) with the standard-practice solution for this
problem class; if your approach is heavier, say where and why it is
worth it.
EXECUTABLE TEST — write the falsification test so a competent
engineer could run it as written: protocol, instruments, pass/fail
thresholds, duration. A test that cannot be run is not a test.
a1_answer:
FEASIBILITY-GROUNDING

PHYSICS CHECK — governing physical relation is thermal expansion: ΔL = α·L·ΔT, where α is the coefficient of thermal expansion (steel ≈ 11×10^-6 /°C), L is the length (spindle length ≈ 500 mm), and ΔT is temperature change. To hold displacement below 10 μm, temperature change must be kept below ΔT = 10×10^-6 / (11×10^-6 × 500) = 1.8°C across the warmup transient.
USER CONSTRAINT: maximum allowable tool center point displacement is 10 micrometers across the 20-minute warmup transient without adding warmup idle cycles
CALCULATED: maximum allowable temperature rise on spindle shaft is 1.8°C based on thermal expansion physics and constraint
ASSUMPTION: spindle length is 500 mm based on typical high-speed machining center spindle dimensions

IMPLEMENTATION BILL — Active cooling system for spindle bearings: 1) Integrated coolant channels in spindle housing with precision flow control valves; 2) Thermoelectric cooling elements (Peltier modules) for localized cooling at bearing locations; 3) Temperature sensors at critical bearing positions (resolution 0.1°C); 4) Closed-loop control system with proportional-integral control algorithm; 5) Heat exchanger to maintain coolant temperature below 20°C; 6) Insulation between heat sources and spindle shaft. All components are off-the-shelf except the integrated spindle cooling channels which require custom manufacturing.
ASSUMPTION: spindle housing can accommodate integrated cooling channels without structural compromise
CALCULATED: cooling capacity required is approximately 150W based on typical bearing heat generation rates

STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY — Standard solution uses extended warmup cycles (30-60 minutes) without active cooling. This implementation adds complexity to spindle design and increases cost by approximately 15-20% due to custom cooling channels and control system. However, it eliminates warmup idle time, potentially increasing machine utilization by 15-25% and improving throughput. The maintenance burden increases slightly due to additional cooling system components, but reliability improves by reducing thermal cycling stress.
CALCULATED: potential throughput improvement of 15-25% based on eliminating warmup cycles
ASSUMPTION: standard warmup cycle is 30 minutes based on industry practice

EXECUTABLE TEST — Protocol: Machine is started from ambient temperature (20°C) with no prior warmup. Tool center point displacement is measured using laser interferometry at 1-minute intervals for 20 minutes. Temperature sensors at bearing positions are recorded simultaneously. Pass/fail criterion: maximum displacement during test must remain below 10 μm at all measurement points. Test duration: 20 minutes plus 5 minutes of stabilization. Required instruments: laser interferometer (resolution 0.1 μm), temperature data logger (resolution 0.1°C), spindle with integrated cooling system. Test repeated 3 times for statistical significance.
USER CONSTRAINT: test duration matches the 20-minute warmup transient specified in the constraint
CALCULATED: measurement interval of 1 minute provides sufficient resolution to capture thermal transient behavior
ASSUMPTION: laser interferometer can be properly aligned to measure tool center point displacement
